[[RunningHead]]

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Twenty Years Ago when Psychoanalytic Inquiry was launched, one of the hopes of the editors was that the journal would contribute to the reduction in the hiatus between the actual occurrences within an analysis and the psychoanalysts' description of those occurrences. Psychoanalysts had great difficulty in describing what actually occurred in the psychoanalytic situation. A principal reason for this discrepancy was that the models that were available to psychoanalysts that could help in understanding and conceptualizing the complexity of the analytic situation were notably incomplete. Today there has been significant change in how analysts think and communicate about the analytic situation because of the depolarization of theoretical positions, the influence of advances in development, neuroscience, and cognition. The psychoanalyst today has a freedom to integrate many concepts from a variety of psychoanalytic models without doing injustice to his or her clinical theory.

During the past 20 years our understanding of therapeutic action has also been enriched. We are able to conceptualize the process far better. Considerable attention has been devoted to the process of change. Models of development have been used to enhance understanding. The concepts of safety and increased capacities for ownership and mastery in the analytic situation are used frequently in describing therapeutic action. Interaction, subjectivity, and enactment have become part of the lexicon of therapeutic action. Some of the developments in neuroscience have already enriched thinking about therapeutic action.

Unconscious communication in the analytic situation remains an area that requires further consideration if our concepts are to continue to become clinically relevant. We still are confronted with a hiatus in the writing and thinking of the psychoanalytic process because insufficient attention is given to the domain of unconscious activity.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Each Author Writes about Unconscious Communication in psycho-analysis from different perspectives and utilizes methodologies from different disciplines. The result is a broadening exploration of unconscious communication in psychoanalysis that can lead to theoretical and technical advances in the field.

Unconscious communication is seen as a partially unconscious process of mutual growth and development occurring within the patient and analyst (Jacobs).

The understanding of unconscious communication that appears magical or uncanny should be considered the result of dynamics that can be understood by utilizing the psychoanalytic method (Kantrowitz).

The findings from child development can promote new ways of looking at unconscious communication in the psychoanalytic situation (Pally).

Including cognition that occurs outside of awareness enriches a systemic approach to unconscious communication. The unconscious is best seen as the result of modalities that are functioning and not whether is in or out of awareness.

Finally there is more in the mind and world than we know or western scientific thinking can explain (Lazar).

All the authors address the limitation of current psychoanalytic thought in offering a more inclusive study of unconscious communication and the importance of learning and borrowing understanding from other disciplines. The future of psychoanalysis will depend on how well we are able to learn from different perspectives and disciplines.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

R. Bristol MD

R. Bristol

R. Bristol  

Our Purpose for this Issue is simple. What might we elicit today from psychoanalysts concerning their views on Freud's historic obsessional neurosis? What is important to them, if anything, about the redefined obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)? What will they say when presented with accumulating, reasonable, and thoughtful nonanalytic clinical and basic science research that suggests a biological basis for OCD and documents the reduction of symptoms by behavioral and pharmacotherapy methods? Given the paucity of analytic claims of cure for OCD, do these findings preempt or negate the Freudian explanation for the obsessional neurosis or other neuroses, when considering psychogenesis (genetic, dynamic, and structural hypotheses), the “choice of neurosis” or the basis of therapeutic action? At present are there any analysts employing psychoanalytic principles to think about a theory for OCD, or are there any that apply the psychoanalytic procedure to treat OCD? Finally, how would they respond to Esman's challenge to integrate the findings of neuroscience within the theory and method of psychoanalysis, and is OCD an example to explore in particular?

We interdigitate these questions in the Prologue to introduce the reader to our diverse authors and their points of reference to these questions. A great deal of evidence supports a biological basis for OCD, but the unique symptomatology, developmental, and traumatic histories have rich, if complicated, psychological appeal that reaches beyond the historic Freudian obsessional neurosis and beyond the means of research and conclusions of current neuroscience.

Esman documents and announces the challenge to integrate psychoanalytic theory and neuroscience of findings, first in 1989— with no response—and again in this issue: analysts have abandoned thinking about OCD or making any claims about its treatment let alone its cause. Lam and Steketee speak of the reduction of symptoms and not their elimination.

Sabine Trautmann-Voigt  

In this rich paper the analysand Annabelle is sent by her analyst to the dance therapist who reports in great detail how Annabelle manages to throw off and—to a certain extent—integrate not only her own life-long misunderstanding but also those of her parents. The reason for Annabelle's referral was straightforward: the analysis had ground to a halt. Words no longer reached her. The reader is reminded of the emotive—relational—motor clusters described in Chazan's and Shahar-Levy's papers. Body image distortions and space misperceptions curtailed this patient's ability to function. When she began to bring her distress to her analytic dance therapy sessions, she could not associate verbally but made use of props her therapist had in store. As she slowly progressed toward true symbolization and expression, her therapist found herself embroiled countertransferentially. The patient's long-suffering mother was remembered as someone who would, or could, only give partial information about the

Prologue

James Fosshage PHD

James Fosshage

James Fosshage  

Comparative Psychoanalysis is at its Best when the same detailed case material is explored from a number of perspectives. It is particularly the case when the presenter and discussants are prominent analysts. To have a senior, well-respected psychoanalyst present detailed clinical material, including process material, all too rare in our psychoanalytic literature, enables other clinicians to enter into, get “a feel” for, and meaningfully address, from their perspectives, the intersubjective interplay. Two such explorations have previously been published in Psychoanalytic Inquiry: the first with clinical material from a classical perspective (1987, Vol. 7, No. 4) and the second from a self-psychological perspective (1990, Vol. 10, No. 4).

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry will be the third comparative case exploration, this time focusing on an object relations clinical presentation. This study served as the First Annual Conference of the Association for Autonomous Psychoanalytic Institutes (AAPI), March 3, 2001, in New York City. We are, indeed, fortunate to have an outstanding roster of psychoanalysts for this study. Jill Savege Scharff, a well-known and respected object relations theoretician and practitioner presents the clinical material. Seven noted psychoanalysts of different perspectives, in turn, discuss Scharff's clinical material. They are Arnold Rothstein, Anne Alvarez, Donnel Stern, Jeff Seinfeld, Frank M. Lachmann, Philip M. Bromberg, and Robert D. Stolorow. Their expertise will cover contemporary conflict, neo-Kleinian, interpersonal/relational, object relations, self psychology, and intersubjective systems perspectives. Each discussant carves out his or her unique understanding of the material with a particular focus on what goes into the process of change. Scharff then replies to the discussants. I close with an Epilogue that highlights the discussants' theoretical nodal points and, more specifically, focuses on their theories of therapeutic action and treatment recommendations.

Epilogue

James Fosshage PHD

James Fosshage

James Fosshage  

All of the Discussants, and probably all of us, resonate with Jill Scharff and her feelings of frustration, disappointment, and impotence that can be generated in difficult treatment engagements. We have seen a sweeping array of theories, understandings, assessments, and treatment recommendations. With Scharff's clinical material serving as the centerpiece, I wish to close by highlighting, ever so briefly, specific theoretical nodal points and, more particularly, by focusing on the theories of therapeutic action and the treatment recommendations of each discussant.

From his perspective of compromise formation theory. Arnold Rothstein views the patient's and analyst's conscious fantasies and behaviors as “related to and derived from complexes of unconscious fantasies.” In addition to drive derivatives, trauma or relational experience influences unconscious fantasies. Conflict is viewed as omnipresent and interminable with shifting multiple determinants. Interpretation and insight are the primary avenues to change. Viewing Ms. Ambar's sadomasochistic character trail as central, Rothstein felt that Jill Scharff should have been more firmly interpretive of Ms. Ambar's sadism.

When addressing change factors, Rothstein also speaks of the importance of the analyst's love of the patient, which includes the analyst's commitment to help, to tolerate, and to understand the patient's sensitivities and aversive responses. Also included is the analyst's willingness to endure the patient's sadistic attacks and to be disturbed by the patient. When Rothstein refers to the analyst's love of the patient, he is referring to new relational experience or, in Scharff's terminology, a new object relationship as a major agent of change. When discussing therapeutic action, however, he seems to back away from the new relational experience and return, instead, to a primary (and traditional) emphasis on interpretation and insight.

Gail Reed PHD

Gail Reed

1199 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10128

Gail Reed  

Although the analyst's way of organizing what he or she hears is influenced by assumptions about human motivation, the analyst's experience in the room with a patient is quite removed from any theories about motivation he or she might hold. So compelling is the clinical interaction that it may only be retrospectively that it is possible to observe how one's theory of motivation influences one's work. Several years ago, on the day before I began working on this paper, I took verbatim notes on the last three sessions of a holiday shortened week to see whether I could discern what assumptions about motivation I was making. I would not describe my theory of motivation as it appears at the end of the essay the way I did at the time I wrote this essay. Today, I would try to integrate drive theory with object relations more explicitly.

[[RunningHead]]

Movement and Meaning

Cary Rick ADTR

Cary Rick

Via Belvedere 28
CH-6962 Viganello, Switzerland

Cary Rick  

Movement analysis receives a new and useful examination in this paper. The fact that all of us always “read” each other's movement behavior as a matter of course is taken for granted. Our verbal language is rife with allusions to bodily behavior, suggesting that there really is such a thing as a language of the body. But one and the same movement can represent many differing aspects of behavior and is heavily dependent on its context. What we experience nonverbally vis-a-vis another person is the executive function of body language like, for instance, “wringing one's hands” or having “shaky knees.” Usually, people will convey nonverbally how they feel about the situation they find themselves in while the other—the recipient of the message—will convey understanding equally nonverbally. Thus, it is always the representation of something that we experience—an embodiment of intent, not language itself. It therefore becomes necessary to distinguish between the implementation and movement itself. These abstractions become helpful in the understanding of many phenomena during treatment situations as demonstrated here.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Elaine Siegel PHD

Elaine Siegel

Elaine Siegel  

The Essays Presented Here constitute only a very brief journey into what might be called “other ways to apply psychoanalytic thought.” The reader has had the opportunity to read about the work of a sophisticated therapist—Michele Rose—who is well versed in both dance therapeutic and psychoanalytic technique. One hopes her work whetted appetites for a word from a ballerina—Ruthanna Boris—who participated in the very beginning of dance as therapy. From this rich beginning, Cary Rick and Yona Shahar-Levy share their theories of how to “write dance” and what that might mean. Saralea Chazan searches for a nonverbal syntax for child therapists while Sabine Trautmann-Voigt puts the reader in the middle of her treatment room where one sees again how psychoanalysis and movement do match and widen the scope of treatment approaches. Joseph Lichtcnberg and Theo Dorpat contribute highly original, creative hypotheses which should make many more patients “treatable.” How to use all this information? Supposing psychoanalytically oriented therapists wish to acknowledge the importance of observing and “translating” the language of the body by incorporating it into their interpretive work: Must they then abandon their technique and become dance movement therapists as well? I hardly think so. Optimally, such colleagues would expose themselves to workshops in which they could “observe with their bodies” what might have been hitherto hidden from their inner view of themselves. Or they might elect to work with a dance movement therapist who will take care of the movement needs of their patients. This can easily produce a split transference unless one is vigilant about interpreting the transference. Dance movement therapists obviously are skilled in the uses of their motility but not all of them know how to keep the analytic dialogue alive.

Toward a Nonverbal Syntax of Play Therapy

Saralea Chazan PHD

Saralea Chazan

5 East 76th Street
New York, NY 10021

Saralea Chazan  

Play therapy receives an innovative, theoretical underpinning for in-depth intervention with children. It is suggested that a new instrument to measure a child's play activity would enhance the understanding of young patients. Interestingly, the word cluster is employed here also to describe categories and components in a child's play. Long clinical experience has shown that nonverbal communication while playing presents its own formal structure, inadvertently adding to the communicative value of any given play situation in therapy. It is possible to pick up intuitively such rich material. But it enriches and makes more plausible treatment efficacy when play activity is measured by the Children's Play Therapy Instrument. The instrument (CPTI), consists of specific, descriptive, structural, and functional scales that can be applied to child patients' play behavior in order to uncover underlying meaning.

This Issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry concerns itself with the vicissitudes of motility and expressive behavior during exploratory psychotherapy. Psychoanalysts may see this as a strange topic, one that, if applied in treatment, might produce acting out or, worse, permit the patient to regress deeply. Yet almost all psychoanalytically oriented therapists have dealt with patients who wish to sit up, rather than using the couch. Amusing vignettes abound about the patient who, for cherished resistances' sake, leaves one foot on the floor, ready for flight, while supine on the couch. To better facilitate recovery from such incidents, analysts might find it useful to give the subject of motility their attention.

Another group of therapists—those whose therapeutic methods are shaped by the arts—have found that using motility as another investigative medium permits more complete understanding of patients.

Freud's dictum that motility must be curtailed in order to foster verbalization has been so emphasized in the training of psychoanalysts that the vicissitudes of this ego apparatus during development and during psychotherapy has found scant attention from psychoanalysts. Child researchers whose work is psychoanalytically informed are the exception.

How a person speaks says as much, if not more, than what they say. Nonverbal cues, such as facial expression, posture and tone of voice are part of all interpersonal relatedness. Nonverbal cues not only express emotion, but also regulate the body physiology, emotions and behaviors between individuals. The homeostatic regulatory mechanisms and affective exchanges between mother and infant proceed nonverbally. Neuroscience data now indicates these same nonverbal mechanisms occur between adults to facilitate attachment, regulate affect and physiology and to provide a sense of being understood. The impact of nonverbal cues is mediated by circuits involving limbic structures in the brain which activate nonverbal cues along with changes in hormone levels, neurotransmitters and the autonomic nervous system. Clinical vignettes are used to illustrate how nonverbal cues function in the analytic treatment setting to shape both transference and countertransference phenomena. Since nonverbal mechanisms can be activated without conscious awareness, neither patient nor analysand may be directly aware of their impact. Analysts must pay attention to their own feelings, behaviors and body sensations as indirect indicators of the affective state and meanings of the patient.

In this paper I suggest that the origins of the “contamination/cleaning” form of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) include a developmental history characterized by marked overprotectiveness allied with parental failure to respond to core aspects of the child's personal reality. The combined effect of these parental behaviors is likely to impede the establishment of a mature conception of the boundary between inner and outer worlds. The consequence of such a deficiency is the persistence of the magical form of thinking which is essential to the production of OCD. In addition, the individual is left with a disruption of personality development, the main features of which include timidity and falseness. The Wolf Man provides an example of both the characteristic development history in OCD and its consequences. Treatment based on this theoretical background may provide benefit not predicted by current psychoanalytic pessimism.

An unorthodox view of the function of primary process is presented with a view to enlarge, rather than diminish Freudian assumptions. One of the basic tenets of Freudian hypothesis was the supposed lack of influence of outside experience upon primary process functions. Obsessive-compulsive disorder has been of central interest to psychoanalysis since Freud's early papers, most particularly in the “Rat Man” case. This early literature spelled out with great clarity the presumed development, psychodynamics, and meaning of obsessional and compulsive symptoms. Unfortunately, since Anna Freud's 1969 review of the subject, virtually nothing has appeared in the psychoanalytic literature that has added tc our understanding of the disorder or enhanced the very limited therapeutic influence of psychoanalysis in such cases. Meanwhile, there has been an avalanche of contributions from biological psychiatry and behavioral psychology that have propounded different theories of pathogenesis and have laid claim to significant therapeutic effectiveness. My understanding of her theoretical viewpoint derives both from my reading of her clinical presentation and from a perusal of The Primer of Object Relations Therapy, which she wrote with her husband (Scharff and Scharff, 1995).

Scharff's object relations perspective casts a wide net. Her emphasis on affective containment and holding—an emphasis I share—harks back to the metaphorical language of Bion and Winnicott. Her assumptions about the pathogenicity of rage and envy and the process of projective identification—assumptions I do not share—derive from Kleinian roots. Her view of psychological life in terms of an endopsychic world of internal objects—particularly internalized bad objects—is strongly reminiscent of Fairbairn's work. In a critique I wrote of Fairbairn's contributions.

The serious consideration of paranormal phenomena, or psi, has not been scientifically respectable in modern intellectual discourse. A skeptical attitude persists despite robust evidence demonstrating the reality of nonlocal phenomena such as telepathy and the impact of mind from a distance. A major obstacle to the thoughtful consideration and integration of this evidence is the fact that paranormal phenomena do not fit within generally accepted models of how the universe works. As neuroscience research has uncovered the genetic/biological basis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), a broad consensus has been reached that behavior therapy and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor are the treatments of choice for the condition. Nevertheless, psychoanalytically informed approaches still have much to offer in an overall treatment plan. The biologically determined symptoms have unconscious meanings to the patient that may lead the patient to be highly invested in maintaining the symptoms. Also, psychodynamic factors may be involved in triggering an exacerbation of the symptoms. Moreover, the compulsions and obsessional thoughts almost always have interpersonal meanings that need to be addressed. Family members and others, including treaters, may feel compelled to accommodate themselves to the illness as a response to coercive behaviors by the patient. Finally, the characteriological features of individuals with OCD tend to undermine treatment efforts in many cases and may require psychoanalytically informed therapy to deal with them.

Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) and perhaps Obsessive Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) are increasingly coming to be viewed as brain diseases treatable by psychopharmacological agents and behavioral therapy. The point of this paper is to illustrate that these conditions probably are on a complemental series, with the proportion of contribution from organic and psychogenic causes variable in each case. The ego of the patient who develops these conditions has always labored badly, whether from psychogenic, constitutional, or neurophysiological factors or a combination of these, and under stress there is a tendency to regression and primitive forms of thinking and wishing. These protect the patient in a magical fashion from a fear of annihilation and dissolution of ego boundaries.

A dramatic long-term case is presented to illustrate the vicissitudes of the development of these conditions along with a whole variety of other symptomatology. This represents a continuing variation in ego functioning as the ego attempts to deal with the vicissitudes of life and perhaps various biological factors. None of these sets of symptoms can be isolated out as a specific “brain disorder” or “disease.” Expert psychopharmacological

Dr. Chessick is Professor of Psychiatry, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL; Training and Supervising Analyst, Center for Psychoanalytic Study in Chicago.

intervention was of little help in this long-term psychotherapy case. In spite of the contentions of those who decry long-term psychoanalytic psychotherapy, this patient would have ended up in a psychotic state without it. Because of the long-term psychotherapy, she was and is able to function reasonably well at her job, and have some sort of self-esteem and autonomy. Psychoanalysis still has much to contribute to our understanding and treatment of so-called OCD and OCPD, and psychoanalytic psychotherapists are urged to continue working with these conditions.

The paper resumes the discussion of obsessional disorders in view of developments that have followed the 1965 Congress of the International Psychoanalytical Association when the last systematic analytic discussion of the Obsessional Neuroses took place. The paper reexamines principal contributions to that congress in an attempt to understand the failure of psycho-analysis to favorably influence the course of these disorders. It notes the subsequent findings of a burgeoning field of child observation that have called attention to the larger infant-caregiver constitutive system within which the intrapsychic phenomenology of the obsessional neuroses is produced and maintained. It draws attention to the crucial impact of the analyst and his causal theories, insufficiently recognized at the time, in the co-determination of the course and outcome of analytic treatment and proposes a contextual systems approach to the reconfigured understanding of normal and pathological development.

The paper discusses the special role of cumulative trauma in the infant-caregiver system on the formation of enduring obsessional and compulsive patterns. It suggests that in the traumatic developmental system, endangerment to the self and

Dr. Bernard Brandchaft is a member of the Clinical Faculty, Department of Psychiatry UCLA School of Medicine, and of the Log Angeles Psychoanalytic Society and Institute.

253

unbearable pain are ever-present threats to the child, and protective strategies, including importantly the processes of pathological accommodation, occupy a primary motivational status. It describes the automatic shaping of subsequent experience by the internalization of sucn processes in template formation. Freud's emphasis on aggression and unconscious guilt in the pathogenesis of the obsessional neuroses system is reexamined in the light of the contextual perspective proposed, and a clinical excerpt is offered to illustrate the thesis of aggression and guilt as contextual products of a traumatic developmental system. Special considerations that enter into the reconfigured analytic treatment of obsessional disorders are proposed, and some observations follow about problems commonly encountered in the new approach.

The paper argues for the systematic extension of the quintessential psychoanalytic tools of empathic-introspective investigation and illumination into the contextualization of inner experience in a fresh approach to the psychoanalytic treatment of these disorders.

The conception of OCD as a brain disease, as it is presented by Dr. Judith Rapoport, is refuted by clinical evidence. This evidence shows obsessive-compulsive symptoms to emerge from a variety of rigid, that is, rule-directed, character. All the well-known obsessive and compulsive symptoms can be derived from character of this sort, in particular from the special, rigid conscientiousness that is its central feature. Deficiencies in the psychoanalytic understanding of symptom formation weaken its case against the reductionistic conception of OCD.

This paper presents a multimodal method of creating OCD, arguing that no single modality of treatment is likely to be appropriate or maximally effective in the treatment of severe OCD. A patient with severe, disabling OCD that had led to a cessation of nearly all ordinary functioning began psychoanalysis at her request, unwilling to try other previously recommended treatments. After the establishment of a very firm, engaged analytic alliance and two years of analysis of issues such as the patient's rage, mistrust, need to control, and commitment to a life of illness, the patient agreed to add behavior modification and medication to her treatment plan. Dr. Fosshage has Asked me to Discuss Dr. Scharff's work, giving particular attention to the question of how change occurs. I pursue my discussion from the perspective of my understanding of compromise formation theory (Brenner, 1982, 1994).

From the perspective of compromise formation theory, the analyst's and analysand's conscious fantasies and behaviors are related to and derived from complexes of unconscious fantasies. These fantasies are conceptualized as structured compromise formations, which are constructed of pleasurable desires, unpleasant affects in the form of anxiety and/or depressive affect, defenses, and self-defeating, self-punitive trends. Jill Scharff's case material is viewed and discussed here from the vantage point of the two partners being an interpenetrating unit held in the grip of an “enactment”—a coconstructed event in which the analyst's participation sometimes becomes so enmeshed with the patient's in an ongoing way that analyst and patient seem to be trapped together in a narrow and concrete tunnel of reality from which they cannot find an escape, gradually making the treatment feel more and more hopeless because it is immune to interpretation of internal conflict. The Selection of the Clinical Material

The Sequence of Sessions I have Selected is from the early midphase of a woman's analysis in which I am working with transference and countertransference in the maternal void. This analysand challenges the value of analysis and tests my confidence. I have made this choice because, being early in the midphase, the treatment process is still open to the effect of the discussants' input.

I waited for sessions that were not close to a vacation in order not to provoke an emphasis on separation and loss. I jotted down notes during and after the sessions, as is my usual habit, and wrote up process notes later. I did not use audiotape because I prefer to rely on my observing ego. I don't pretend that it is possible to have 100 percent accuracy, even with audiotape, and I realize that what I am giving you to work with is my version of what happened. I prefer to use the narrative form to convey the analytic process, and I hope it is not falsely persuasive of one point of view.

Prologue

R. Bristol MD

R. Bristol

R. Bristol  

Aaron H. Esman (1989) is the first psychoanalyst to show the dissimilarities between the current psychiatric, behavioral, and neuroscience research—and their derivative theories and therapeutic strategies—regarding the obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and the historic obsessional neurosis of Sigmund Freud (1894), 1895b, 1896, 1907, 1909, 1913a, b, 1926).

The 30-year evolution of Freud's views about the obsessional neurosis are fundamental to his general psychological theory of mind that followed his initial study on hysteria. Even early on, Freud's (1895a, 1909, 1913b) study of the obsessional neurosis established a remarkable excursion into the unconscious. These assumptions about psychoanalytic theory are relevant today and include psychic determinism, repression, unconscious drive derivative, psychic conflict, symptom formation, primary and secondary defenses, unconscious memory, return of the repressed, compromise formation, and displacement (Jones, 1953, pp. 278-279, 282). The “Rat Man” and “Wolf Man” are landmarks of the psychoanalytic case study that remain central to Freud's genetic, dynamic, and topographic metapsychology. Ernest Jones (1955) points out that the obsessional neurosis was elemental in Freud's evolving technique, a model for analysts today: “his timing of interpretations, his characteristic use of analogies to illustrate a point,… the preliminary guesses he would make privately which might subsequently be either confirmed or disproved, and altogether the tentative manner in which such piecemeal work proceeded” (p. 230). Freud's (1904) procedure of free association established the corner stones of psychoanalytic method: transference, resistance, and the theory of repression. Thus Freud's innovation of mental structure and function owe a considerable debt to his study of the obsessional neurosis.

This paper presents a review of the empirical literature on OCD, focusing on treatments developed on the basis of behavioral learning theories. The discussant begins by describing her British Object-Relations perspective. She emphasizes the difference between obstructive or critical forces within the personality which are best described as a part of the self and those which are felt by the patient to have a quality of otherness about them: the latter are better conceptualized as internal objects since this is closer to the patient's subjective experience. The author stresses the importance—in Scharff's patient's inner world—of the useless maternal—and impotent paternal—object. ‘Stupid’ rather than ‘bad’ objects can affect introjective processes and limit the patient's intellectual functioning because, where the world is seen as uninteresting and unstimulating, it is therefore not worth attending to nor learning from. The author also made a further point. She saw the patient's repetitive bitter self-criticisms, although partly arising out of deprivation, depression, and abuse, as also possibly containing an element of masochistic pleasure in suffering and failure. This would raise delicate technical issues in balancing a sensitive approach to the real suffering with a clearly stated recognition of the addictive repetitive masochistic quality which accompanies it and which may be blocking recovery.

Scharff's Account of a Nine-Session Sequence in the middle phase of a four times a week analysis demonstrates the suffering of the maternal void in the transference-countertransference. Neither patient nor analyst is turned on or excited by these analytic sessions. Scharff honestly and courageously describes her Internal processes and responses to the patient. She reports feeling abusive, abandoning, useless, intrusive, penetrative. There is agreement on the part of patient and analyst that the sessions feel unproductive, unrewarding, that little work is getting done. Each partner in the analytic dyad complains of the other's passivity. Scharff experiences the patient as waiting for the analyst to give her a jump start. The patient acknowledges this and waits. The analyst recognizes that much of the analytic work is being done by her internally and that she is frustrated by the patient's resistance to working analytically. She imagines the patient's wringing her heart so that she can feel the patient's heartbreak and feel responsible for her suffering.

Scharff and Scharff (1992) have distinguished containing and holding. Containing refers to the clinician's Internal processes in dealing with the patient's projected overwhelming and intolerable psychic states.

Prologue

Morton Shane MD

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

Human Motivation has been a Central Feature of psychoanalysis from its inception. Hidden motivation is what intrigued the founders of psychoanalysis. Breuer and Freud sought to discover the cause of mysterious symptoms and developed important explanations that hinged on unconscious motivation. When Freud abandoned the trauma theory of the neurosis, he put drive motivation at the center of psychoanalytic thought, which continues for many to this day. Over the years there have been many other theorists who have altered Freud's dual drive theory in various directions, including putting emphasis on object seeking rather than drive seeking, on expanding fundamental motivations well beyond the dual drives, and in addition, reviving the centrality of trauma in the formation of psychopathology.

This issue is dedicated to a contemporary view of the state of human motivation in the theory and practice of psychoanalysis.

Gail Reed, in her paper, “Patients' Motivations and the Analyst's Experience,” illustrates her understanding of motivation in psychoanalysis by presenting three detailed clinical vignettes chosen from her practice preceding the weekend in which she undertook to write her essay. In presenting her work this way, she highlights her approach to theory, that clinical experience precedes and takes precedence over theoretical assumptions. Nevertheless, she is forthright in presenting these theoretical assumptions at the end of each of the vignettes. She assumes that free associations are verbal derivatives of drives and that the interplay of drive derivatives and defenses are the main constituents of conflict. She finds concepts of regression, projective identification, and the illusion of omnipotent control to be important and manifest in transference and countertransference.

Toward a Theory of Entelechy

James Grotstein

522 Dalehurst Avenue

James Grotstein  

The psychoanalytic theory of motivation needs to be recast in a vitalistic holistic (holographic) language that liberates it from its constraints to the drives and expresses that it constitutes an indivisible function of being and continuing to being-alive. In the development of his thesis the author retraces the history of Freud's acquaintance with the idea and points out that Freud required a theory of unconscious motivation or intentionality to account for the creation of unconscious phantasies-and ultimately for psychic determinism. Psychic determinism became the template for the concept of psychic responsibility.

The author attempts to place the concept of motivation into the more all-inclusive and more vitalistic notion of entelechy so as to express its more holographic and numinous nature. A discussion of the relationship between motivation and its associated entities is made. These include volition, will, intentionality, agency, and autochthony. It is pointed out that motivation can be considered to be holographic in so far as one can consider the whole individual to be motivated, but along side this consideration one sees motivation within each portion

Psychoanalysts' interest in the need for exploration and assertiveness, originally investigated empirically during the 1940s and 1950s, has recently been revived (Lichtenberg, 1989: Lichtenberg, Lachmann, and Fosshage, 1992, 1996). Exploratory-assertive motivation has been seen as a basic motive that interacts with several other forms of motivation to fulfill and regulate the person's basic needs, direct interpersonal relations, and maintain the organization of the self. In this paper, it is reasoned that recognizing and systematically and actively integrating the pervasive influence of this powerful motivational system outside, as well as within, psychoanalytic sessions can usefully redefine and broaden the scope and reshape the thrust of many psychoanalytic interventions. Three specific areas of psychoanalytic technique are probed in relation to exploratory-assertive motivation: enhancing patients' feelings of self-efficacy, shading interpretations toward action, and promoting

Back to Basics

The Psychoanalytic Conceptualization of Motivation

Mervyn Peskin MD

Mervyn Peskin

1040 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10028

Mervyn Peskin  

Reconsideration of motivation, a fundamental concept in psychoanalytic theory, engages us with basic assumptions and postulates of our field and draws us to the borders with neighboring scientific elaborations of the design, structure, and function of the mind. This paper presents a concept of motivation from a perspective in modern conflict theory and correlates this concept with current thinking in evolutionary biology. The challenges that this correlation raises for all psychoanalytic approaches to motivation are discussed. Natural selection has fundamentally organized motivation in accord with the principle of inclusive fitness. Adaptive motivations of self-interest achieved through social success are paramount. In mind sciences there is a growing appreciation of the innately modular mind with mounting evidence for domain and content-specific evolved psychological mechanisms, the modern term for instincts. In regard to motivation in modern conflict theory, evolved mechanisms and predispositions are innately linked to pleasure-unpleasure and include, importantly, motivations of self-interest. The pleasure-unpleasure principle regulates motivation throughout life. Early mother-child interactions are vital to the development and contextualization of motivation;
